πόλις ἐρειπομένη πλείστας τε ὅσας αὐτοῖς, καὶ μὴν καὶ εὐρεῖς τὰς καταδύσεις

pass_a_gloss: [...] of those in it, because of its having been made wholly desert. And it must be known that the tribes of the Saracens, both reaching as far as the Assyrians themselves and occupying the innermost desert, he names Arabs. For they have the land of the Arabs as neighbour. And it is likely that the Saracens from Arabia themselves also roam about, mixed together, the deserts of the Assyrians. [Lemma, Isaiah 13:21-22:] And beasts will rest there, and the houses will be filled with echo. And sirens will rest there, and demons will dance there. And donkey-centaurs will dwell there, and hedgehogs will nest in their houses. It comes quickly and will not delay. It is somehow always dear to the wild among animals to make the deserted parts of places a dwelling, and a city falling into ruins makes for them very many, and indeed wide, lurking places, self-roofed and improvised, and found as if of their own accord from what happened. And in deserts and the silent among places a certain thin echo, and as if from the excessive silence, I know not how, rises and enters the hearing of those at rest. So beasts will rest, he says, and the houses will be filled with echo; that is, having no inhabitant at all, they will acquire the echo fitting to desolations. And demons, he says, will dance there. For they say that these too somehow love to haunt especially the quiet among places, and to make there a leisurely lodging, as it were. Sirens, I think, he calls the birds that know how to sing well, or according to the edition of the Hebrews, the owl. The wild among donkeys he named donkey-centaurs; and indeed hedgehogs, those among mice bristling as it were with sharp thorns. And all these things would fittingly suit cities or houses wholly deserted. And he adds to these that it comes quickly and will not delay, either putting into the Assyrians a more bitter worry, or making no small comfort for those from the blood of Israel. For since they were in captivity, and expected to be released when Cyrus made war on the Babylonians together with Persians and Medes, he promises them a quick release from the painful things, and that the things in prayers will not be for long postponement, but will run as it were at the foot of the word. [Lemma, Isaiah 14:1-3:] And the Lord will have mercy on Jacob, and will yet choose Israel, and they will rest on their land, and the sojourner will be added to them. And he will be added to the house of Jacob; and nations will take them and bring them into their place. And they will inherit, and will be multiplied on the land of God, into male slaves and female slaves; and those who took them captive will be captives, and those who lorded over them will be lorded over; and it will be on that day [the section breaks off mid-word].
pass_b_english: …of those in it, because it has been laid utterly waste. It should be known that he calls “Arabs” the Saracen tribes, which reach as far as the land of the Assyrians itself and occupy the innermost desert; for they have the land of the Arabs as their neighbour. And it is likely that the Saracens from Arabia themselves also roam, mingled together, through the deserts of the Assyrians.

“And wild beasts will rest there, and the houses will be filled with echo. And sirens will rest there, and demons will dance there. And donkey-centaurs will dwell there, and hedgehogs will make their nests in their houses. It comes quickly and will not delay” (Isaiah 13:21-22).

Wild animals somehow always like to make deserted places their home, and a city falling into ruin gives them a great many hiding places, wide ones too, roofed over by themselves and makeshift, found, as it were, by chance and of their own accord. In deserts and silent places a faint echo, I do not know how, rises as if out of the very depth of the silence and steals into the ears of those who keep still.

So wild beasts, he says, will rest there, and the houses will be filled with echo; that is, having no one at all living in them, they will come to hold the echo that belongs to desolate places. And demons too, he says, will dance there. For they say that these also especially like to linger in quiet places and to make them a kind of leisurely lodging.

By “sirens” he means, I think, the birds that know how to sing sweetly, or, according to the Hebrew edition, the owl. The wild donkeys he has called “donkey-centaurs”; and by “hedgehogs” he means those mice that bristle, as it were, with sharp spines. All these would fittingly suit cities or houses that are wholly deserted.

To these he adds that “it comes quickly and will not delay” (Isaiah 13:22). He does this either to put a sharper anxiety into the Assyrians, or else to make it no small comfort to those of Israel's blood. For since they were in captivity and were expecting to be set free when Cyrus marched against the land of the Babylonians with the Persians and the Medes, he promises them a swift release from their troubles: what they prayed for would not be put off for long, but would follow, as it were, close on the heels of the word.

“And the Lord will have mercy on Jacob and will yet choose Israel, and they will rest on their own land, and the sojourner will be joined to them and will be joined to the house of Jacob. And nations will take them and bring them into their place; and they will take possession of them, and they will be multiplied on the land of God as male and female slaves. And those who took them captive will be captives, and those who ruled over them will be ruled. And it will be on that day…” (Isaiah 14:1-3).

choices.why: The object is the Saracen tribes; it is they whom the prophet calls Arabs, not the Assyrians or the desert.
rejected: the Assyrians and the innermost desert are called Arabs

choices.why: The ruins give the animals ready-made covered hiding places.
rejected: self-made roofs (reads as if the animals built them)

choices.why: The Septuagint word is kept in the lemma; Cyril then explains it as songbirds or, from the Hebrew, the owl.
Literal form of the Septuagint word, which Cyril then explains as wild donkeys.
The Septuagint word for the resident alien who joins Israel.
